newsitem.title: USA: White House defends aide in new fundraising flap.
newsitem.headline: White House defends aide in new fundraising flap.

text.p: The White House insisted on Thursday that Hillary Rodham Clinton's top aide did not break a law against fundraising on federal property by accepting a $50,000 political donation in the U.S. executive mansion.

"He (President Bill Clinton) expects all White House employees to follow the procedures approved by the legal counsel and that's what Maggie apparently did," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters during a presidential trip to this Midwestern city.
He referred to Maggie Williams, the first lady's chief of staff, who is at the centre of the latest fundraising row.
Attorney General Janet Reno, meanwhile, said she still saw no reason to appoint an independent counsel to investigate the controversy despite a mounting clamour that she do so.

At her weekly news briefing in Washington, Reno, a member of Clinton's Cabinet, maintained that the legal threshold for an independent counsel had not been reached, despite new revelations involving Williams and Vice President Al Gore.
Her comments meant in practice that the probe will continue to be handled by Clinton's own Justice Department.

On Capitol Hill, the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee put off for one week a vote on a resolution demanding a appointment of an independent counsel. Such a resolution would not legally force Reno to appoint a counsel but it would sharply increase pressure on her to do so.

Republican committee chairman Orrin Hatch of Utah, hoping to win some bipartisan backing for the measure, agreed to the delay at the request of Democrats who said they wanted more time to review the resolution's language.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott promised action within a week, saying: "We feel very strongly that there's more than enough reason to have an independent counsel. We don't quite understand why the attorney general has not moved to do that."

The latest fund-raising furore erupted on Wednesday night when officials confirmed that Williams had accepted a $50,000 campaign donation in March 1995 in the White House from Johnny Chung, a Clinton booster with Asian ties.

White House officials insisted she had merely been an innocent conduit between Chung and the Democratic National Committee and had not broken laws prohibiting political cash transactions on federal property.

McCurry took that position when questioned by reporters en route to Michigan, saying federal law and regulations "very clearly make a distinction between accepting and receiving contributions and merely handling contributions. You are allowed to direct the contribution to its destination."
He said he personally would not have accepted the money and "would have directed them directly to the DNC," but made clear he was not criticising Williams for having done so.

Reno said the threshold requirement for an independent counsel -- specific, credible evidence of a criminal violation by a high-ranking official -- had not been reached. But she did not rule out seeking a counsel later.

"What is so important in all of this is that we take it very carefully, we do it thoroughly, we consider the case history, we consider the legislative history and we do it the right way, without somebody staring into the camera and saying something is inevitable or not inevitable," she said. "... These matters have to be reviewed in the most objective manner possible, without politics and without pressure."
The Williams row followed one involving Gore, who acknowledged he had made fund-raising calls from his office in 1995 and 1996. He too maintained he had broken no law.
In each episode critics cite a section of federal law that makes it illegal for any government official to solicit or receive any contribution on federal property.
But a Justice Department official said the law had been rarely enforced, with the last prosecution in 1913.
